acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors

NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain out of proportion, fever, spreading erythema, crepitus** → evaluate necrotizing perineal infection urgently
Posterior midline fissure common; lateral/multiple fissures suggest Crohn disease, infection, or malignancy
Internal hemorrhoids lie above dentate line; prolapse may require manual reduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fissure causes internal sphincter spasm and local ischemia; hemorrhoids represent enlarged vascular cushions
Cryptoglandular infection creates abscess; persistent epithelialized tract can become a fistula

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Inspection first**, gentle DRE/anoscopy when tolerable; do not force painful fissure examination
Deep pain without visible lesion → CT/MRI for occult abscess; recurrent fistula → pelvic MRI
Rectal bleeding with anemia, weight loss, bowel change, or screening indication → colon evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Fiber, fluids, stool softening, **sitz baths**; fissure → topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem
Refractory chronic fissure → botulinum toxin or lateral internal sphincterotomy after continence-risk assessment
Internal hemorrhoids persisting despite conservative measures → rubber-band ligation; advanced prolapse → surgery
★ Abscess → **incision and drainage**; antibiotics added for cellulitis, systemic illness, or immunosuppression
Fistula → colorectal surgery; painful thrombosed external hemorrhoid within 72 hours → consider excision

rows.label: Complications
items: Abscess recurrence, fistula, sepsis; sphincter injury → fecal incontinence
Chronic bleeding → iron deficiency; pruritus → excoriations and secondary infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid straining and prolonged toilet sitting; gentle cleansing, dry skin, barrier ointment for seepage

rows.label: Mimics
items: Anal cancer: persistent irregular ulcer/mass, biopsy required
Proctitis: urgency, tenesmus, mucous discharge
Pinworm: nocturnal itch, especially children; tape test

table.title: Local patterns
rows: Tearing defecation pain; bright blood on paper
Recurrent purulent drainage from external opening

anorectal-disorders.evidence: Not checked online; established colorectal teaching.

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery, incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Partial obstruction may still permit stool or diarrhea; bowel movements do not exclude early obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.name: Dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.scope: Uninvestigated dyspepsia (age < 60 test-and-treat vs age >= 60 endoscopy), Helicobacter pylori testing and eradication, gastric and duodenal ulcers
dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.core: Epigastric discomfort may reflect functional dyspepsia or acid-peptic ulceration; age and bleeding risk determine noninvasive testing versus endoscopy.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: H pylori, NSAIDs/aspirin; smoking impairs healing
Prior ulcer bleeding, anticoagulants, older age amplify NSAID harm; severe physiologic stress causes ICU ulcers

rows.label: Clues
items: Epigastric burning, early satiety, nausea; meal timing cannot reliably distinguish ulcer location
★ Hematemesis/melena, progressive dysphagia, persistent vomiting, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia → **alarm evaluation**
Sudden rigid abdomen → perforation; early satiety with recurrent vomiting → gastric outlet obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: H pylori or prostaglandin depletion weakens mucosal defenses against acid-pepsin injury
Antral-predominant infection increases acid; corpus-predominant inflammation may cause atrophy

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ New dyspepsia **≥60 years → upper endoscopy**; younger high-risk/alarm presentations assessed individually
★ Under 60 without concerning features → **urea breath or stool antigen test**
Hold PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics/bismuth 4 weeks before active-infection testing; serology cannot confirm eradication
Gastric ulcer → biopsy to exclude malignancy; duodenal ulcers rarely malignant
Refractory/recurrent multiple ulcers + diarrhea → fasting gastrin with careful PPI interpretation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ H pylori → **14-day bismuth quadruple**: PPI + bismuth + tetracycline + metronidazole
Avoid empiric clarithromycin/levofloxacin regimens unless susceptibility demonstrated
Negative infection test or persistent symptoms after eradication → PPI trial; functional symptoms may need TCA
Stop NSAID; ulcer healing → PPI; active bleeding → resuscitation, IV PPI, urgent endoscopic hemostasis
Perforation → IV fluids, ceftriaxone/metronidazole, urgent surgery; no elective diagnostic endoscopy

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhage, perforation, penetration, outlet obstruction; H pylori → gastric cancer, MALT lymphoma

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Confirm eradication ≥4 weeks after antibiotics** with breath/stool test, off PPI as above
Necessary NSAID + high GI risk → concurrent PPI; use lowest effective NSAID exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Biliary colic: episodic RUQ pain, gallstones on ultrasound
ACS: exertional epigastric pressure, ischemic ECG/troponin findings

dyspepsia-and-peptic-ulcer-disease.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG H pylori update (2024)](https://gi.org/journals-publications/ebgi/schoenfeld_sep2024/); dyspepsia age threshold established ACG/CAG teaching.

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation; cholecystectomy → bile-duct injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.name: Gastroesophageal reflux disease
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.scope: Clinical diagnosis, empiric PPI trial, lifestyle measures, alarm symptoms, Barrett esophagus screening, 24-hour pH monitoring
gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.core: Heartburn and acid regurgitation after meals or recumbency suggest reflux; complications or diagnostic uncertainty change the testing pathway.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Obesity, pregnancy, hiatal hernia, smoking; drugs reducing lower esophageal sphincter tone
Late large meals and individual food triggers exacerbate symptoms

rows.label: Clues
items: Sour taste, nocturnal symptoms, chest discomfort; chronic cough/hoarseness nonspecific and often multifactorial
★ **Dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss**, persistent vomiting, anemia → endoscopy
Exertional or acute chest pain requires cardiac evaluation before attributing symptoms to reflux

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Transient lower sphincter relaxation and impaired barrier allow gastric contents into esophagus
Acid exposure → erosions; chronic injury may produce intestinal metaplasia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical symptoms without alarms → **8-week empiric once-daily PPI trial**
Alarm features or failed treatment → upper endoscopy; biopsies evaluate alternative mucosal disease
★ Unproven GERD + normal endoscopy → **ambulatory pH monitoring off PPI**
Proven GERD with refractory symptoms → impedance-pH testing on PPI after optimizing use
Manometry evaluates motility and precedes antireflux surgery; not the primary reflux diagnostic test

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Omeprazole 30–60 minutes before breakfast**; verify adherence before escalation
Intermittent mild symptoms → antacid or famotidine; persistent breakthrough → optimize/split PPI schedule
Weight reduction if overweight; avoid meals within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate bed head
Objective reflux with troublesome regurgitation despite optimized drugs → fundoplication or selected endoscopic intervention
Severe erosive esophagitis → long-term PPI or surgery; step down uncomplicated controlled disease

rows.label: Complications
items: Erosive esophagitis, peptic stricture, Barrett esophagus, adenocarcinoma
Stricture → endoscopic dilation plus acid suppression; dysplastic Barrett requires specialist eradication treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: Barrett screening: chronic reflux + ≥3 additional risks: male, >50, White, tobacco, obesity, first-degree family history
Smoking cessation and symptom-directed trigger reduction; routine endoscopy unnecessary for every reflux patient

rows.label: Mimics
items: Achalasia: solids and liquids dysphagia, impaired sphincter relaxation
Eosinophilic esophagitis: atopy, food impaction, eosinophilic biopsy
Functional heartburn: normal reflux burden and no symptom association

gastroesophageal-reflux-disease.evidence: Not checked online; established ACG reflux and Barrett screening teaching.

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency; elevated BUN/creatinine ratio supports upper source

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Active exsanguination → blood immediately regardless of hemoglobin; cardiac ischemia → individualize higher threshold
Severe life-threatening anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; persistent bleeding after endoscopy → IR/surgery
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

gastrointestinal-bleeding.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACG lower GI bleeding 2023](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36735555/), [ACS transfusion guidance 2025](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.11.009).

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults may have apathetic presentation
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → radioactive iodine uptake, except pregnancy/lactation
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

hypothermia-and-frostbite.name: Hypothermia and frostbite
hypothermia-and-frostbite.scope: Accidental hypothermia, core rewarming techniques, frostbite stages, rapid warm water bath rewarming, delayed surgical debridement
hypothermia-and-frostbite.core: Cold exposure can cause systemic core-temperature depression and local freezing injury; stabilize the patient before thawing threatened tissue.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Wet/windy exposure, homelessness, alcohol/drugs, extremes of age, immobility
Hypothyroidism, hypoglycemia, sepsis, malnutrition; frostbite risk rises with tight boots and vascular disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Core temperature <35°C** defines hypothermia; use low-reading core thermometer
Shivering, slowed cognition → later bradycardia, hypoventilation, absent shivering, coma
ECG: Osborn J waves; severe disease predisposes to ventricular arrhythmia
Frozen tissue: pale, waxy, hard, insensate; after thaw, blister characteristics help estimate depth

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heat loss exceeds production → enzyme, cardiac, and CNS dysfunction
Local ice crystals and endothelial injury cause microvascular thrombosis; refreezing greatly worsens damage

rows.label: Dx
items: ABCs, core temperature, bedside glucose, ECG; evaluate electrolytes, renal function, trauma, intoxication
Check pulse/breathing carefully because rates can be extremely slow; monitor continuously
Deep frostbite: specialist perfusion imaging helps salvage/prognosis after rewarming, not before stabilization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove wet clothes, insulate, **gentle handling**; warm trunk before limbs, avoid rough movement
★ **32–35°C, alert** → insulation/external heat; <32°C → **active external + internal rewarming**
Warmed IV fluids prevent further cooling; severe instability/arrest → extracorporeal rewarming when available
★ Frostbite: **37–39°C circulating water** until thawed, only when refreezing can be prevented
Analgesia, loose dressings, separate digits, tetanus update; deep injury → urgent thrombolysis/iloprost evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Afterdrop, hypotension, dysrhythmia, rhabdomyolysis; tissue loss, neuropathic pain, cold sensitivity
★ **Delay amputation until demarcation** except infection/sepsis or another surgical emergency
No rubbing, direct dry heat, or walking on thawed feet when avoidable; prophylactic antibiotics not routine

rows.label: Prevention
items: Dry layered insulation, warm shelter, buddy checks, adequate food; avoid alcohol in cold exposure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonfreezing trench foot: prolonged wet exposure without tissue freezing
Raynaud phenomenon: episodic reversible vasospasm without frozen tissue

hypothermia-and-frostbite.evidence: Frostbite guidance checked 2026-10-30: [WMS 2024](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/10806032231222359); hypothermia content established teaching.

increased-intracranial-pressure.name: Increased intracranial pressure
increased-intracranial-pressure.scope: Cushing triad, papilledema, ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, herniation syndromes, hyperosmolar therapy
increased-intracranial-pressure.core: Progressive headache, vomiting, or depressed consciousness from raised intracranial pressure requires rapid distinction between mass effect, hydrocephalus, and idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Trauma, intracranial bleeding, tumor, cerebral edema, CNS infection, obstructed CSF flow
VP shunt: blockage or infection; IIH: obesity, reproductive-age women, tetracyclines, retinoids

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning/Valsalva headache, papilledema, diplopia from sixth-nerve palsy; infants may have bulging fontanelle
★ **Cushing triad**: hypertension/widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, irregular respirations; late dangerous finding
Uncal herniation → ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral weakness; tonsillar herniation → respiratory arrest
IIH: pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations; shunt failure: recurrent headache, vomiting, lethargy

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed skull volume: excess tissue, blood, or CSF raises pressure after compensatory reserve exhausted
Cerebral perfusion pressure = MAP − ICP; falling perfusion worsens ischemia and edema

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Unstable/acute deficit → **noncontrast head CT**; papilledema with stable suspected IIH → MRI + MRV
★ **No LP before excluding mass effect/obstructive hydrocephalus** when concerning signs present
IIH: normal imaging aside from supportive findings, normal CSF composition, opening pressure ≥25 cm H₂O
Shunt failure → head imaging, shunt series, urgent neurosurgery; normal ventricular size does not exclude obstruction

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Herniation concern → **airway support, head elevation, IV hypertonic saline or mannitol**, urgent neurosurgery
Avoid hypoxia/hypotension; brief controlled hyperventilation only as bridge for impending herniation
Hydrocephalus → CSF drainage/shunt revision; mass lesion → definitive decompression
Dexamethasone for tumor-associated vasogenic edema; no corticosteroids for traumatic brain injury
IIH → weight loss + acetazolamide; threatened vision → optic nerve fenestration or CSF diversion

rows.label: Complications
items: Permanent visual loss, ischemic injury, herniation, death
Hyperosmolar agents → electrolyte/renal disturbances; CSF devices → infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid causative drugs in IIH; follow visual fields and optic discs
Shunt education: prompt evaluation for recurrence or fever; injury prevention

rows.label: Mimics
items: Migraine: normal fundus and no progressive focal/mental-status findings
Cerebral venous thrombosis: venous obstruction on MRV, not idiopathic disease

increased-intracranial-pressure.evidence: Not checked online; established neurocritical care and IIH diagnostic principles.

informed-consent-and-capacity.name: Informed consent and capacity
informed-consent-and-capacity.scope: Decision-making capacity, informed consent, emergency exception (implied consent), refusal of treatment, AMA discharge
informed-consent-and-capacity.core: A capable adult may accept or refuse treatment after understanding its benefits, material risks, alternatives, and consequences of refusal.

rows.label: Principle
items: ★ Capacity: **understand, appreciate, reason, communicate choice**; specific to decision, fluctuating
Competence: legal determination; diagnosis, age, or disagreement alone does not establish incapacity

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Explain benefits, material risks, alternatives/no treatment; **qualified interpreter and teach-back**
Correct delirium, intoxication, pain, communication barriers; reassess capacity
AMA request: assess capacity, explore barriers, offer safer plan, document discussion and follow-up

rows.label: Don't
items: Capable refusal → respect choice, including life-saving treatment; avoid coercion or abandonment
No valid consent → possible **battery**; signed form alone insufficient

rows.label: Exceptions
items: ★ Emergency + incapacity + no available surrogate/directive → implied consent for necessary treatment
★ Parents refuse minor's life-saving transfusion → **treat emergency**; seek court authority if feasible
Incapacity without emergency → authorized surrogate; involve patient to remaining ability

rows.label: Traps
items: Psychiatric illness does not automatically remove capacity; assess the specific decision
Suicide danger may justify protective detention despite expressed desire to leave
New material procedure or substantially changed risk → renewed consent discussion

informed-consent-and-capacity.evidence: Not checked online; established consent/capacity ethics; emergency and minor-consent law varies by jurisdiction.

mesenteric-ischemia.name: Mesenteric ischemia
mesenteric-ischemia.scope: Acute mesenteric ischemia, chronic mesenteric ischemia, ischemic colitis, CTA abdomen, colonoscopy
mesenteric-ischemia.core: Intestinal hypoperfusion causes severe abdominal pain; early examination and lactate may appear deceptively reassuring.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: AF, recent MI, valvular disease → embolism; diffuse atherosclerosis → arterial thrombosis
Shock, heart failure, vasopressors → nonocclusive ischemia; hypercoagulability → mesenteric venous thrombosis

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Pain out of proportion** to abdominal examination; sudden onset especially with embolism
Nausea, diarrhea, later bloody stool; guarding/rebound suggests transmural infarction
Right-sided colonic disease or severe pain without bleeding → investigate proximal mesenteric occlusion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen supply failure injures mucosa before serosa; bacterial translocation and necrosis follow
Collateral flow usually protects intestine until acute major occlusion or multivessel chronic disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CTA abdomen/pelvis with arterial and venous phases** immediately for suspected acute ischemia
Do not delay lifesaving contrast imaging solely because of renal dysfunction
CBC, metabolic panel, lactate/ABG; normal early lactate does not exclude disease
Avoid colonoscopy with peritonitis, perforation, or suspected gangrene; minimal insufflation when safe

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute mesenteric: NPO, **IV saline, piperacillin-tazobactam, unfractionated heparin**; urgent vascular/surgical consult
★ **Peritonitis or infarcted bowel → emergency laparotomy**, resect nonviable bowel and restore flow
Arterial occlusion without peritonitis → urgent endovascular/open revascularization based on anatomy and expertise
Nonocclusive disease → restore perfusion, reduce vasoconstrictors; selected catheter-directed papaverine
Isolated mesenteric venous thrombosis without infarction → anticoagulation

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis, multiorgan failure, death
Short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection; reperfusion injury, recurrent thrombosis
Ischemic colitis can heal with segmental stricture

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Anticoagulate AF when eligible**; smoking cessation, statin, atherosclerotic risk reduction
Treat low-flow triggers promptly; thrombophilia evaluation for selected venous thrombosis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Infectious colitis: exposure/fever, stool pathogen identification
Pancreatitis: epigastric/back pain with lipase elevation
Perforated viscus: early rigid abdomen/free air; bowel obstruction: transition point on CT

table.title: Chronic disease versus colonic ischemia
rows: Postprandial pain, food fear, weight loss
Cramps then hematochezia; older low-flow patient
Fluids, bowel rest; ceftriaxone/metronidazole if moderate/severe

mesenteric-ischemia.evidence: Colonic disease checked 2026-10-30: [ACG colon ischemia guideline](https://acgcdn.gi.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/ACG-Colon-Ischemia-Guideline-Summary.pdf); acute mesenteric treatment: established emergency framework.

peripheral-artery-disease.name: Peripheral artery disease
peripheral-artery-disease.scope: Claudication, aortoiliac (Leriche) disease, critical and acute limb ischemia
peripheral-artery-disease.core: Atherosclerotic limb hypoperfusion ranges from exertional claudication to rest pain, tissue loss, or abrupt limb-threatening arterial occlusion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, age, CKD, hypertension, dyslipidemia; coronary/cerebrovascular atherosclerosis commonly coexists
AF, aneurysm, graft disease, hypercoagulability predispose acute occlusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Diminished pulses, cool shiny skin, hair loss, dependent rubor, distal nonhealing ulcers
★ **Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia** → acute limb ischemia
Sensory/motor deficits signal threatened limb; do not await all six findings

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Fixed arterial narrowing limits exercise perfusion; progressive failure reduces resting tissue oxygenation
Acute embolus/thrombus prevents collateral compensation, rapidly injuring nerves and muscle

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ABI ≤0.90** confirms PAD; 0.91–0.99 borderline; >1.40 suggests noncompressible arteries
Exertional symptoms with normal resting ABI → exercise ABI; noncompressible vessels → toe-brachial index
Duplex, CTA/MRA define anatomy when revascularization planned; urgent Doppler exam in acute ischemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic PAD: **clopidogrel or aspirin + high-intensity statin**, smoking cessation, structured exercise
Cilostazol improves claudication; contraindicated in any heart failure
Refractory disabling claudication → revascularization; chronic limb-threatening ischemia → prompt limb-salvage evaluation
★ Acute ischemia → **IV unfractionated heparin and immediate vascular consultation**; salvageable limb → urgent reperfusion
Low bleeding risk, symptomatic/postrevascularization → low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin; no full anticoagulation solely for PAD

rows.label: Complications
items: Gangrene, infection, amputation; MI/stroke often dominate long-term mortality
Reperfusion → compartment syndrome, hyperkalemia, rhabdomyolysis; irreversible limb may require primary amputation

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Daily foot inspection**, protective footwear, diabetic foot care, BP/glucose control
Avoid thermal injury to insensate feet; antithrombotic plan after procedures based on bleeding risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Spinal stenosis: flexion relieves walking pain, pulses preserved
Venous ulcer: medial ankle, edema, pulses intact; neuropathy: sensory loss without ischemic pulse findings

table.title: Clinical stages
rows: Reproducible exercise pain relieved by rest
Buttock claudication, erectile dysfunction, weak femorals

potassium-disorders.name: Potassium disorders
potassium-disorders.scope: Hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, cardiac membrane stabilization, shift therapy, elimination
potassium-disorders.core: Potassium abnormalities can cause weakness and fatal arrhythmias; stabilize cardiac risk while identifying the cause and correcting total-body balance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hyperkalemia: AKI/CKD, RAAS blockers, potassium-sparing diuretics, tissue lysis, insulin deficiency
Hypokalemia: GI losses, loop/thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, insulin/beta-agonists, magnesium depletion

rows.label: Clues
items: Flaccid weakness, paralysis, palpitations; symptoms may be absent despite dangerous levels
★ **K ≥6.5 mmol/L, ECG changes, or rapid rise** → emergency; normal ECG not reassuring

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Extracellular K changes alter membrane excitability and cardiac conduction
Acidosis/insulin deficiency shift K outward; intracellular shifts can coexist with severe total-body depletion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG + repeat potassium**, creatinine, glucose, bicarbonate, magnesium; assess drugs and acid-base status
Hemolysis, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis → pseudohyperkalemia; repeat atraumatic draw if clinically compatible
Hypokalemia: urine K distinguishes renal wasting from extrarenal loss; interpret with BP/acid-base pattern
Do not delay treatment for confirmatory blood draw when malignant ECG changes present

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Hyperkalemic ECG toxicity → **IV calcium gluconate**; protects myocardium without removing potassium
★ Shift K inward: **IV insulin + dextrose**, nebulized albuterol; bicarbonate mainly with significant acidosis
Remove K: loop diuretic if urine output, selected binders; urgent dialysis for severe refractory/renal-failure cases
Mild/stable hypokalemia → oral KCl; <2.5, arrhythmia, paralysis, or no oral access → monitored IV replacement
★ **Correct magnesium deficiency** for refractory low K; never give IV potassium push; monitor glucose after insulin

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventricular arrhythmia, cardiac arrest, respiratory muscle failure
Overcorrection, rebound dyskalemia; insulin-induced hypoglycemia; IV potassium extravasation/phlebitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Review supplements/salt substitutes; monitor K/creatinine after diuretic or RAAS-drug changes
Treat diarrhea/vomiting and underlying mineralocorticoid disorders; replace ongoing losses

rows.label: Mimics
items: Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexic weakness without explanatory electrolyte pattern
Periodic paralysis: episodic shifts, sometimes thyrotoxicosis; avoid excessive replacement causing rebound

table.title: ECG patterns
rows: Peaked T → PR prolongation → wide QRS/sine-wave
Flat T, ST depression, prominent U waves

shock.name: Shock
shock.scope: Hypovolemic, cardiogenic, distributive (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic), obstructive, fluid resuscitation, vasopressors
shock.core: Circulatory failure causing tissue hypoperfusion; normal blood pressure does not exclude early shock.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hemorrhage, GI losses, MI, infection, allergen exposure, spinal injury, thromboembolism
Recent surgery, immunosuppression, indwelling devices increase occult infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Tachycardia, altered mentation, oliguria, cool mottled skin; distributive forms may initially feel warm
★ **Anaphylaxis**: rapid airway swelling, wheezing, hypotension; skin findings may be absent
Neurogenic: hypotension with **bradycardia**, warm skin after spinal cord injury

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Oxygen delivery falls below demand → anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation
Distributive vasodilation → relative hypovolemia despite normal total body fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Bedside ultrasound**: cardiac function, pericardial fluid, RV dilation, lung sliding, volume assessment
Serial lactate, capillary refill, urine output; CBC, chemistry, ECG, troponin; cultures if infection suspected
Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP ≥65 plus lactate >2 despite volume resuscitation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway/oxygen, IV access; **balanced crystalloid**, dynamic fluid-response reassessment; restrict with pulmonary congestion
★ Hemorrhage → **control bleeding + balanced blood products**; avoid large crystalloid loads
★ Septic shock → antibiotics within 1 hour, drainage/debridement; crystalloid 30 mL/kg within 3 hours
★ Persistent septic hypotension → **norepinephrine**, MAP ≥65; add vasopressin, then epinephrine; refractory → hydrocortisone

rows.label: Complications
items: AKI, ischemic hepatitis, DIC, ARDS, bowel ischemia, multiorgan failure
Excess fluids → edema; vasopressors → digital/mesenteric ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early infection treatment, catheter hygiene, VTE prophylaxis, hemorrhage control
After anaphylaxis: trigger avoidance, epinephrine autoinjector, allergy referral

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal syncope: transient bradycardia, rapid recovery supine
Hypoglycemia: low bedside glucose, improvement with dextrose

table.title: Hemodynamics and cause-directed rescue
rows: Decompress pneumothorax; drain tamponade; reperfuse PE

skin-cancer.name: Skin cancer
skin-cancer.scope: Actinic keratosis, squamous cell carcinoma, basal cell carcinoma, melanoma, photoprotection and sunscreen
skin-cancer.core: Changing pigmented lesions or persistent keratinizing, pearly, or ulcerated growths require examination and tissue diagnosis rather than empiric reassurance.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: UV exposure, fair skin, sunburns, tanning beds, older age; immunosuppression particularly increases SCC
Melanoma: numerous/atypical nevi, family/personal melanoma history; may arise without a preexisting nevus
Chronic wounds/scars predispose SCC; acral melanoma occurs regardless of skin pigmentation

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Melanoma: **ABCDE**—asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter, evolution; ugly-duckling lesion
Diameter >6 mm concerning, but smaller evolving lesions still require biopsy
Amelanotic melanoma may be pink; inspect soles, palms, nail beds; nail pigment extending onto fold concerning
Rapid growth, bleeding, nonhealing ulcer, fixation, neurologic symptoms, nodes → aggressive or advanced disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: UV-induced DNA damage → keratinocyte malignancy; melanocyte transformation causes melanoma
AK represents dysplastic keratinocytes with potential progression to invasive SCC

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious melanoma → **full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow margins** to measure Breslow depth
Partial biopsy acceptable when complete excision impractical; avoid superficial sampling that prevents staging
Suspected keratinocyte carcinoma → shave, punch, or excisional biopsy deep enough to assess invasion
Breslow thickness/ulceration guide melanoma staging; sentinel-node discussion generally at ≥0.8 mm or ulceration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Localized invasive cancers → **surgical excision**; high-risk/recurrent facial BCC/SCC → Mohs
★ Melanoma → **wide local excision after diagnostic biopsy**; margins depend on depth
Advanced melanoma → specialist immunotherapy, selected BRAF-targeted drugs; avoid destructive treatment before diagnosis

rows.label: Complications
items: BCC: extensive local destruction, rare metastasis; SCC: nodal metastasis, especially high-risk sites/immunosuppression
Melanoma: distant metastases, including brain; immunotherapy → colitis, endocrinopathies, pneumonitis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Broad-spectrum SPF ≥30**, reapply every 2 hours/outdoors after swimming; shade, protective clothing, no tanning
Self-examination, postcancer follow-up; suspicious lesions require evaluation despite uncertain population-screening benefit

rows.label: Mimics
items: Seborrheic keratosis: waxy stuck-on plaque; atypical lesions still biopsy
Dermatofibroma: firm papule with dimple sign
Benign nevus: stable symmetric uniform appearance

table.title: Nonmelanoma patterns
rows: Assess high-risk features and regional nodes
Pearly rolled edge, telangiectasia, central ulcer
Treat despite slow growth; local invasion

skin-cancer.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AAD melanoma guidance](https://www.aad.org/member/clinical-quality/guidelines/melanoma); established keratinocyte-cancer and photoprotection teaching.

valvular-heart-disease.name: Valvular heart disease
valvular-heart-disease.scope: Aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, mitral stenosis, mitral regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse, physical exam, echocardiography, surgical and transcatheter replacement
valvular-heart-disease.core: Murmur timing, location, radiation, and loading maneuvers localize valve disease; symptoms and ventricular response determine intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Aging calcification/bicuspid valve → AS; rheumatic disease → MS
Endocarditis, aortic root dilation/dissection → AR; ischemia, prolapse, chamber dilation → MR

rows.label: Clues
items: Exertional dyspnea, pulmonary edema, reduced exercise tolerance; abrupt deterioration suggests acute regurgitation
★ **Exertional syncope, angina, or HF** with obstruction → severe symptomatic disease
Squatting/handgrip increase regurgitant murmurs; standing/Valsalva makes MVP click earlier

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stenosis produces upstream pressure overload; regurgitation produces chamber volume overload
Acute regurgitation lacks compensatory dilation, rapidly elevating filling pressures and reducing forward output

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TTE Doppler** defines anatomy, severity, EF, chamber dimensions, pulmonary pressures
Severe AS: velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40, or valve area ≤1 cm²; discordance requires reassessment
Severe MS: valve area ≤1.5 cm²; TEE for thrombus before balloon intervention or uncertain anatomy
★ Acute murmur with shock → **urgent echocardiography**; TEE if endocarditis/dissection suspected

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe AR/MR → **urgent surgery**, stabilize with afterload reduction/diuresis if BP permits
Severe primary MR: **EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm** triggers intervention even without symptoms
Secondary MR → optimize HF treatment first; selected persistent severe cases benefit from transcatheter edge-to-edge repair
Avoid excessive preload reduction in severe AS; symptomatic relief never replaces needed valve intervention

rows.label: Complications
items: Heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, AF, systemic embolism, endocarditis
Mechanical prosthesis: thrombosis/bleeding; bioprosthesis: structural degeneration

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Warfarin for mechanical valves**; no DOAC substitution; rheumatic MS with AF also requires warfarin
Prosthetic valve or prior endocarditis → selected dental prophylaxis; native isolated MVP does not qualify
Periodic echo and symptom review; treat rheumatic fever to prevent recurrent valve injury

rows.label: Mimics
items: HCM: systolic murmur increases with Valsalva/standing
Aortic sclerosis: ejection murmur without significant gradient; flow murmur: normal valve anatomy

table.title: Valve signatures and definitive options
rows: Early diastolic decrescendo; wide pulse pressure
Suitable symptomatic rheumatic valve → balloon commissurotomy

venous-thromboembolism.name: Venous thromboembolism
venous-thromboembolism.core: Unilateral swollen leg or sudden unexplained dyspnea with pleuritic pain; pulmonary embolism severity determined by hemodynamics, not clot size.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Immobilization, surgery, malignancy, estrogen, pregnancy/postpartum, previous VTE, inherited thrombophilia

rows.label: Clues
items: DVT: asymmetric calf tenderness, warmth; PE: tachycardia, hypoxemia, hemoptysis, sometimes normal oxygen saturation
Syncope, elevated JVP, cool extremities → impending RV failure; normal chest radiograph does not exclude PE

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Stasis/endothelial injury/hypercoagulability → venous clot; pulmonary obstruction → V/Q mismatch, RV pressure overload

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Wells/pretest probability** first; very low-risk + PERC-negative → no testing
★ Low/intermediate probability → **D-dimer**; negative excludes; positive/high probability → **CT pulmonary angiography**
Age >50: D-dimer threshold age × 10 ng/mL FEU; contrast contraindication → V/Q scan
DVT → compression US; negative proximal scan + persistent suspicion → repeat in 1 week

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Oxygen/support circulation; unstable and unsafe for CT → bedside **echo**; high suspicion/delayed imaging → anticoagulate
★ Most stable VTE → **apixaban/rivaroxaban**; pregnancy → LMWH; severe renal failure → UFH
Lysis contraindicated/fails → catheter thrombectomy/surgical embolectomy; active intracranial bleeding precludes lysis
Acute proximal DVT/PE + absolute anticoagulation contraindication → temporary **IVC filter**, remove when feasible

rows.label: Complications
items: Postthrombotic syndrome; persistent dyspnea → evaluate chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
Anticoagulation/thrombolysis → bleeding; heparin → HIT

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Major transient trigger → **3 months** anticoagulation; unprovoked/persistent risk → extended course if low bleeding risk
Hospital prophylaxis: LMWH; active bleeding → intermittent pneumatic compression; early mobilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cellulitis: predominantly skin erythema, portal of entry
Ruptured Baker cyst: posterior knee symptoms, cyst on US
Pneumonia: focal infiltrate and infectious prodrome

table.title: Treatment branches; 2026 PE guidance uses categories A–E
rows: Stable; low PESI/sPESI; no RV injury
Normotensive + RV dysfunction and/or troponin elevation
Sustained SBP <90 mm Hg or shock
